b.t: A **knowledge graph (KG)** represents information as **entities** (nodes) connected by **relationships** (edges). The basic fact unit is a **triple**: `(subject, predicate, object)`, e.g. `(Marie Curie, WON, Nobel Prize)`.

r: nodes and edges have labels and key-value properties
everything is a triple; uses URIs and ontologies (RDFS/OWL)

i: **Degree** — number of edges attached to a node (in-degree / out-degree for directed graphs).
**Path** — a sequence of edges; a **hop** is one edge traversal.
**Neighbourhood** — nodes within k hops.
**Community** — a densely connected group of nodes.
**Ontology / schema** — allowed entity and relation types.

b.t: Vector RAG retrieves chunks that *look similar* to the query. Some questions need **connections** that no single chunk states:

i: **Multi-hop**: "Which university did the founder of the company that acquired X attend?"
**Aggregation / global**: "What are the main themes across 5,000 support tickets?"
**Relationship reasoning**: "How is supplier A connected to the recall?"

b.t: A graph makes those connections explicit and traversable.

i: KGs store facts as entity–relationship–entity triples.
Property graphs (Cypher/GQL) and RDF (SPARQL) are the two main models.
Graphs help with multi-hop, relational and corpus-wide questions where vector similarity struggles.

b.t: Traditional KG construction needed hand-written NLP pipelines. LLMs can now extract entities and relations directly from text.

i: **Chunk** the documents.
**Extract** entities (with types and descriptions) and relationships (with descriptions/weights) from each chunk using an LLM prompt or structured output.
**Resolve entities** — merge duplicates ("IBM", "I.B.M.", "International Business Machines") using string similarity, embeddings and/or an LLM.
**Store** nodes and edges in a graph database, keeping links back to the **source chunks** (provenance).
**Enrich** — compute embeddings for nodes, detect communities, summarise.
**Schema-free** extraction captures anything but yields noisy, inconsistent relation names.
**Schema-guided** extraction restricts entity types (`Person`, `Company`, `Drug`) and relations (`WORKS_AT`, `TREATS`) for cleaner, queryable graphs.

b.t:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Relation(BaseModel):
    source: str
    source_type: str
    relation: str
    target: str
    target_type: str

class Extraction(BaseModel):
    relations: list[Relation]

extractor = llm.with_structured_output(Extraction)
result = extractor.invoke(
    "Extract (source, relation, target) triples using types Person, Company, Product.\n\n"
    "Text: Ada Lovelace founded Acme in 2019. Acme makes the Nova drone."
)
# relations: (Ada Lovelace)-[FOUNDED]->(Acme), (Acme)-[MAKES]->(Nova drone)
Tools that do this for you: LangChain's `LLMGraphTransformer`, LlamaIndex `PropertyGraphIndex` extractors, Neo4j's LLM Graph Builder, Microsoft GraphRAG, LightRAG.

i: Extraction requires an LLM call per chunk (often several) — the dominant indexing cost.
Entity resolution errors split or wrongly merge nodes, breaking multi-hop paths.
Always keep provenance so answers can cite original text.
LLM-based extraction turns chunks into entities and relations; entity resolution merges duplicates.
Schemas make graphs cleaner and easier to query.
Indexing cost is dominated by LLM extraction calls.

b.t: **GraphRAG** (Microsoft Research, 2024) builds a knowledge graph from a corpus and pre-computes **community summaries** to answer both specific and **global** questions.

i: Split documents into **text units** (chunks).
LLM-extract **entities**, **relationships** and optional **claims/covariates**; summarise descriptions of entities that appear many times.
Run hierarchical community detection with the **Leiden** algorithm to partition the graph into nested communities (levels 0, 1, 2...).
Generate a **community report** (LLM summary) for every community at every level.
Embed entity descriptions (and text units) for vector lookup. Outputs are stored as Parquet tables.

r: find entities relevant to the query (via embeddings), then gather their neighbours, relationships, claims, community reports and source text units into the context
specific entity questions ("What does Acme make?")
map-reduce over community reports: each report produces partial answers with importance scores (map), then the best are combined (reduce)
holistic questions ("What are the main themes?")
starts like a light global search over top community reports to produce an initial answer and follow-up questions, then runs local searches for each follow-up
questions needing both breadth and detail
plain vector search over text units

b.t: Plain vector RAG answers "What are the top 5 themes in this dataset?" poorly because no single chunk contains the answer. GraphRAG's community reports are pre-computed summaries of every region of the graph, so global search can synthesise across the **whole corpus**.

i: Indexing is **expensive** (many LLM calls for extraction and reports) and must be re-run or updated incrementally as data changes.
Global search over many reports is costly at query time; **dynamic community selection** prunes irrelevant communities first.
**LazyGraphRAG** (Microsoft, late 2024) defers LLM summarisation to query time, cutting indexing cost dramatically.

b.t:
pip install graphrag
graphrag init --root ./ragtest          # creates settings.yaml + prompts
graphrag index --root ./ragtest         # build the graph & community reports
graphrag query --root ./ragtest --method global --query "What are the main themes?"
graphrag query --root ./ragtest --method local  --query "Who founded Acme?"

i: GraphRAG = LLM-extracted graph + Leiden communities + community reports.
Local search for entity questions; global (map-reduce over reports) for corpus-wide themes; DRIFT combines them.
Indexing cost is high; LazyGraphRAG and dynamic community selection reduce cost.

t: LightRAG and Other Graph-Based RAG Variants

b.t: **LightRAG** (2024, HKU) is a lighter-weight graph RAG:

i: Extracts entities and relations per chunk and stores them in a graph plus vector indexes of entities and relations.

**Dual-level retrieval**: *low-level* keys target specific entities and their attributes; *high-level* keys target broader themes and relations. The LLM extracts both kinds of keywords from the query.
Query modes: `naive` (plain vector), `local` (entity-focused), `global` (relation/theme-focused), `hybrid` (local + global) and `mix` (graph + vector).
Supports **incremental updates** by merging new entities/edges into the existing graph — no full rebuild like classic GraphRAG.

b.t: Inspired by the hippocampus: builds a KG from passages and uses **Personalized PageRank** seeded by query entities to find related passages across hops — strong on multi-hop QA with a single retrieval step.

i: **KG-augmented vector RAG**: retrieve chunks by vectors, then expand with graph neighbours of the entities they mention.
**Text2Cypher / Text2SPARQL**: the LLM writes a graph query that is executed for precise answers (counts, paths, filters).
**GraphRetriever / graph traversal retrievers**: vector-search seed nodes, then traverse k hops.
**RAPTOR** (tree, not graph): recursive clustering + summarisation of chunks into a tree (see RAG Architectures).

r: Precise structured questions over curated data

i: LightRAG uses dual-level (entity + theme) retrieval and incremental graph updates.
HippoRAG uses Personalized PageRank for multi-hop retrieval.
Text2Cypher answers precise structural questions by generating graph queries.

b.t: Cypher uses ASCII-art patterns: `()` for nodes, `-[]->` for relationships.

r: create only if the pattern doesn't exist

b.t: Neo4j (and others like Memgraph, FalkorDB, ArangoDB, Amazon Neptune, Kùzu-style embedded graphs) support **vector indexes** on node properties, enabling hybrid retrieval: vector search finds entry nodes, Cypher expands their neighbourhood.

CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('chunk_embeddings', 5, $queryEmbedding)
YIELD node, score
MATCH (node)-[:MENTIONS]->(e:Entity)-[r]-(related)
RETURN node.text, e.name, type(r), related.name, score;

i: Cypher patterns: `(n:Label {prop})-[:REL]->(m)`; MERGE for idempotent ingestion.
Variable-length `[*1..3]` and `shortestPath` power multi-hop queries.
Graph DBs with vector indexes enable vector-seeded graph expansion.

b.t: An LLM translates natural language into Cypher using the **graph schema**:

from langchain_neo4j import Neo4jGraph, GraphCypherQAChain

graph = Neo4jGraph(url="bolt://localhost:7687", username="neo4j", password="...")
graph.refresh_schema()                          # node labels, relationship types, properties
chain = GraphCypherQAChain.from_llm(
    llm=model, graph=graph,
    validate_cypher=True,                        # fix relationship directions
    allow_dangerous_requests=True,               # you acknowledge the LLM writes DB queries
)
chain.invoke({"query": "How many products does Acme make?"})

i: Use a **read-only** database user — never let generated queries write.
Provide the schema and **few-shot examples** of question → Cypher.
Validate/repair queries; retry on syntax errors; limit result sizes.
`LLMSynonymRetriever` — expands query keywords/synonyms and matches nodes.
`VectorContextRetriever` — vector search over nodes, then expands paths.
`TextToCypherRetriever` / `CypherTemplateRetriever` — generated or templated Cypher.

b.t: Expose several tools to an agent — `vector_search`, `graph_neighbours(entity)`, `run_cypher(query)` — and let it choose per question. This handles both fuzzy ("tell me about…") and precise ("how many…") questions.

i: Text2Cypher needs schema context, examples, validation and a read-only DB user.
LlamaIndex offers synonym, vector-context and text-to-Cypher graph retrievers.
Agents combining vector and graph tools cover both fuzzy and precise questions.

t: Evaluating Graph RAG and When to Use It

i: **Answer quality**: correctness, faithfulness, comprehensiveness, diversity (GraphRAG's paper used LLM-judged comprehensiveness, diversity and empowerment vs vector RAG).
**Multi-hop accuracy** on datasets like HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA.
**Graph quality**: entity extraction precision/recall, duplicate rate, relation accuracy.
**Cost & latency**: indexing tokens, query tokens, query time.

b.t: When Graph RAG is worth it

i: ✅ Highly connected domains (supply chains, biomedical, legal, finance, IT dependencies).
✅ Questions about relationships, paths, multi-hop reasoning, or entire-corpus themes.
✅ Need for explainability (show the path used).
❌ Simple FAQ or lookup over independent documents — vector or hybrid RAG is cheaper.
❌ Rapidly changing data without budget for re-indexing.
❌ Very small corpora where long context suffices.
Start with hybrid vector RAG and an eval set.
Identify failing question types (multi-hop, global).
Add a graph for those: entity extraction + graph expansion, or GraphRAG global search for summaries.
Route questions to vector, graph or hybrid retrieval with a classifier or agent.
Evaluate answer quality, multi-hop accuracy, graph quality and cost.
Graph RAG pays off for connected data and relationship/global questions.
Route questions: not every query needs the graph.
